summary: Duplicate values make linear worst-case search unavoidable: an all-equal absent-target array can differ from a valid rotated array containing one target at any uninspected position. The current ambiguity-shrinking search matches that bound.

optimality.argument: Consider an array of n copies of one non-target value. Until a position is inspected, that position could instead contain the sole target and the array would still be a valid rotation of a non-decreasing array. Proving absence therefore requires Omega(n) inspections in the worst case. The current search either discards a sorted half or removes duplicate boundary copies, and every boundary moves inward at most n times, giving O(n) time.

replacement_checks.evidence: The all-equal absent instance and an instance with one target at any unchecked position are both legal rotated non-decreasing arrays but require different boolean results.
Informative iterations halve or discard a side; ambiguous equal-boundary iterations increment left and decrement right, so the inclusive interval can shrink only O(n) times.
The source-fidelity-verified examples cover present and absent targets in the same duplicate-containing rotation; black-box real-test execution passed all five existing ordinary correctness checks.
